summary: Specifies a restricted profile of Internet mail protocols for exchanging voice messages between voice processing server platforms. It sets a minimum common set of features for interoperability. It obsoletes RFC 2421 and RFC 2423.

plainLanguage.summary: The Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) lets voice messaging systems exchange messages using Internet mail. It sets shared rules for addresses, voice and fax content, delivery reports, and transport.

subtitle: A restricted Internet-mail profile for exchanging voice messages between messaging systems.

tldr.problem: Traditional voice messaging systems often lack the features of general-purpose email systems, so they need a shared minimum for exchanging messages.
tldr.mechanism: VPIMv2 profiles SMTP and MIME, defines voice-oriented addresses and headers, and packages audio, optional fax, and forwarded messages in Multipart/Voice-Message.
tldr.outcome: The profile sets a minimum common feature set for interoperable systems. RFC 3801 obsoletes RFC 2421 and RFC 2423; it clarifies version 2 without changing its protocol.

today: RFC 3801 is a Draft Standard published in June 2004 and obsoletes RFC 2421 and RFC 2423. The RFC says this revision clarifies VPIM version 2 without changing its protocol.

sections.title: The Voice Messaging Profile
sections.content:
RFC 3801 defines VPIM version 2, a restricted profile of Internet multimedia messaging for voice-processing servers. These systems historically had telephone interfaces and limited support for text, message headers, and Internet mail features.

VPIM aims to make few changes to existing mail protocols while defining enough common behavior for systems to interoperate. It is designed mainly for exchanges between voice messaging systems and VPIM-aware clients, not for ordinary commercial email clients.
sections.plainLanguage: VPIM applies Internet mail rules to voice messaging systems with limited email features. It defines a common baseline so those systems can exchange messages.

sections.title: Addresses and Special Mailboxes
sections.content:
A VPIM address has a local part identifying a mailbox and a host part identifying the machine. Short numeric local parts SHOULD be used because many telephone interfaces rely on keypads; an international public number follows E.164 and has at most 15 digits.

Every system MUST have a postmaster mailbox for diagnostics. The special address non-mail-user marks an originator who cannot receive replies, such as a telephone answering service; systems MUST NOT offer a reply and MUST reject messages addressed to it with status 5.1.1.

Distribution lists are optional. If a system cannot list all recipients, it SHOULD omit recipient headers rather than provide an incomplete list.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses use a mailbox name and a machine name, and numeric mailbox names are easier to enter by telephone. A non-mail-user address tells the receiver that a reply is not possible.

sections.title: Message Header Fields
sections.content:
VPIM permits a defined set of message headers, and systems MUST accept and ignore headers they do not recognize. The sender's full address MUST appear in From, and Date, Message-ID, Received, MIME-Version, and Content-Type have required roles.

To and Cc may list recipients only when the full list is known; a blind-copied recipient MUST NOT be disclosed. Reply-To SHOULD NOT be sent because voice systems commonly support one originator.

A Private Sensitivity value means the receiver MUST prohibit forwarding. If the system cannot assure privacy, it MUST send a negative delivery status notification with status 5.6.0.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers identify the sender, recipients, time, and message. A Private sensitivity value means the receiving system must not forward the message.

sections.title: Voice, Fax, and Forwarded Content
sections.content:
A VPIM message uses a Multipart/Voice-Message container with a required boundary and version parameter; version 2.0 identifies this profile. The container has the same semantics as Multipart/Mixed and may contain only the profiled audio, image, and Message/RFC822 content types unless systems have a bilateral agreement.

Audio/32KADPCM is the default voice encoding, at 32 kbits per second, and receivers MUST decode it. A voice part is marked inline and uses a voice parameter to identify whether it is the main message, a spoken name, a subject, or a notification.

Fax uses the TIFF-F profile in Image/TIFF with application=faxbw. A system that cannot render fax SHOULD retain the voice content and discard the fax. Forwarded messages SHOULD use a Message/RFC822 part.
sections.plainLanguage: The container labels the main voice message and can include fax or forwarded mail. The default audio format is Audio/32KADPCM, which every conforming receiver must decode.

sections.title: Delivery and Disposition Reports
sections.content:
A Delivery Status Notification reports delivery, non-delivery, or delay. VPIM systems MUST send and receive DSNs, and unless requested otherwise a non-delivery DSN MUST be sent when delivery fails. Its human-readable part SHOULD provide a spoken status, though text is allowed.

A Message Disposition Notification reports what happened after a message reached a mailbox, such as being played or deleted. Systems SHOULD support MDN requests and responses. An unsupported media type can be reported with status 5.6.1.

If the return path is empty, as for a telephone answering message, a DSN MUST NOT be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: A delivery report tells the sender whether a message arrived, while a disposition report can say what happened after arrival. Reports can include spoken status for users who access messages by phone.

sections.title: SMTP Transport and Extensions
sections.content:
VPIM messages travel between voice messaging systems using Extended SMTP. The SMTP envelope carries delivery information such as sender and recipient addresses; conforming systems MUST implement the mandatory SMTP and ESMTP commands.

DSN and SIZE extensions MUST be supported. ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES and PIPELINING SHOULD be supported, while CHUNKING and BINARYMIME MAY be supported. If binary transport is available, audio and fax SHOULD use it; otherwise they MUST use Base64.

DSN support is needed at every hop for consistent delivery reports. If a relay must downgrade and cannot pass a DSN request, it is RECOMMENDED to continue delivery but it MUST notify the originator.
sections.plainLanguage: VPIM sends messages using SMTP and uses its extensions for message size and delivery reports. Audio and fax use binary transport when available or Base64 when it is not.

sections.title: Conformance and Security
sections.content:
VPIM defines transport and content conformance. A transport-conformant system forwards messages without losing information and provides delivery notifications; a content-conformant system generates and interprets the profiled message structures.

Voice messaging systems and protocol-conversion gateways are expected to meet both areas. Relays are expected to meet transport rules and create conforming delivery reports when delivery fails.

The RFC identifies risks from spoofed sender information, unsolicited voice mail, and message disclosure. It introduces no security mechanism beyond the profiled mail protocols and does not prevent using Internet security protocols to encrypt or authenticate messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems carry messages, while others create and interpret their contents, so VPIM sets separate rules for each role. Its security discussion covers sender spoofing, unwanted messages, and privacy expectations.
